newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: ASEAN ministers set to decide membership issue.
newsitem.headline: ASEAN ministers set to decide membership issue.

text.p: Foreign Ministers of the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) forum gathered in Malaysia on Friday for a weekend meeting to decide when to admit Burma, Cambodia and Laos into the influential grouping.

ASEAN decided last year to give membership to the three countries some time in 1997. On Saturday, the foreign ministers from Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam will decide exactly when that will happen.

Malaysia, this year's chairman, has been pressing for the induction to take place at ASEAN's annual meeting in July. The admission ceremony is tentatively on the schedule for the July meeting, Asian diplomats said.

But concerns about political strife in Cambodia, clashes between Buddhists and Moslems in Burma and Rangoon's latest swoop against democracy campaigners could persuade the ministers to delay the admission to year's end, diplomats said.
The United States and the European Union have openly pressured ASEAN to delay Burma's membership because of its human rights record.
"It's very hard to read," one Western diplomat said. "My personal guess is that it will still happen in July."
Another diplomat said he thought the question was still open. "I think it very much depends on the personal chemistry of the ministers when they meet."
If the decision is to delay admission, Cambodia would likely be cited as the reason.

A senior Cambodia official said earlier this week that the legislature's inability to meet, due to feuding among the country's political factions, has prevented the country from ratifying key documents required for membership.

New members are required to sign ASEAN's Treaty of Amity and Friendship, another treaty declaring the region a nuclear weapons-free zone and a third document detailing its readiness to join the ASEAN Free Trade Area.
But diplomats noted ASEAN officials have previously said that ratifying the documents was a technical matter and would not block a political decision to admit the three.

"Cambodia could be the smokescreen they hide behind if the decision is to delay. The ratification issue isn't crucial," the Western diplomat said. "They can fudge these things. This is the land of fudge."

ASEAN governments have been used to fending off pressure from the West over Burma, but now they are beginning to hear from local groups, as well. An influential Malaysian Moslem group this week urged Burma's admission be deferred, holding Rangoon's military rulers responsible for clashes between Buddhists and Moslems in March that led to the destruction of a number of mosques.

Malaysian activist groups held a protest on Friday against Burma's membership outside the Malaysian Foreign Ministry. Malaysia has been keen to have the three new members join at the July meeting so it could unveil a new ASEAN logo during the group's 30th anniversary celebrations. The logo features 10 rice stalks joined together, representing the 10 members.
ASEAN was founded in 1967 at the height of the Vietnam War as an anti-Communist bulwark in the region.

Kuala Lumpur is thought to be less eager for the admission to take place at December's summit in Malaysia. Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad has invited China, South Korea and Japan to the summit -- those three plus ASEAN make up his controversial East Asia Economic Caucus, an Asia-only grouping that Washington is not pleased about.
Malaysia would prefer not to have the Burma issue adding more diplomatic aggravation at that summit, diplomats said.
